comparison: Both evaluate the temporal trend finding (C5, C34, C35) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing (logistic regression, p<0.001) and proper handling of pseudoreplication. Peer reviewers accept the finding without challenge, noting the encouraging decrease over time.

Both evaluate subdiscipline differences (C6, C36-C38) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights appropriate statistical testing (χ² test, p<0.001) and biological plausibility. Peer reviewers accept the finding that cell-oriented disciplines show higher rates of problematic images.

Both evaluate the web application tool (C9, C76-C78) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes clear technical specifications and reproducibility. Peer reviewers acknowledge the tool positively, noting it is well-documented and open source, though Reviewer 2 mentions limitations with Ishihara test images.

Both evaluate model comparison methodology (C39-C42) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate cross-validation and clear performance metrics. Peer reviewers accept the CNN approach as appropriate and note the extensive hyperparameter evaluation (C43 also included in peer review).

Both evaluate computational analysis of color pairs (C2, C24-C27) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical testing (Hartigans' Dip Test, p<0.001) but mentions the 85.6% figure requires context. Peer reviewers accept these computational metrics as valid preliminary screening, implicitly accepting the distinction between computational detection (85.6%) and manual determination (12.8%).

Both evaluate manual review methodology and mitigation factors (C3, C30-C33), but reach different conclusions. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED despite noting lack of inter-rater reliability metrics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 raising significant concern that deuteranopes were not engaged as stakeholders, creating uncertainty about whether spatial separation and labeling truly address accessibility needs.

Both address the manual review finding of 12.8% problematic images (C4, C28, C29) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval acknowledges the systematic approach by two independent reviewers. Peer reviewers accept this key finding without challenge, with all reviewers citing the ~13% figure as valid.

Both evaluate CNN performance on eLife data (C7, C44) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes strong performance with AUPRC 0.77 being good for imbalanced problems. Peer reviewers accept the performance metrics (0.89 AUROC, 0.77 AUPRC) without question.

Both evaluate the error analysis of misclassifications (C45-C47) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval finds this post-hoc analysis valuable, suggesting the model may sometimes be more accurate than human reviewers. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the methodology demonstrating understanding of model failures.

Both evaluate reduced performance on PubMed Central data (C8, C49, C63) but with different emphasis. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting honest reporting and substantial performance drop (AUPRC 0.77 to 0.39) indicating limited generalizability. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with all reviewers identifying this as a significant limitation questioning the tool's generalizability, though not disputing the reported metrics.

Both evaluate comparative findings between eLife and PubMed Central datasets (C51-C53) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the lower prevalence (5.2% vs 12.8%) and higher grayscale proportion provide context. Peer reviewers accept these comparative findings and the grayscale explanation without challenge.

Both evaluate the explanation for reduced generalizability (C64, C66) and reach the same conclusion: SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the authors appropriately acknowledge that single-journal training limits generalizability. Peer reviewers agree with this interpretation, with Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly stating that using images from a single journal limits generalizability.

Both evaluate limitations related to simulation-based methodology (C60, C61, C70-C72), but reach different conclusions. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, commending the authors' transparency about using simulations and single severity threshold. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 explicitly critiquing the missed opportunity to engage deuteranopes as stakeholders and questioning whether the 80% severity threshold is inclusive enough.

Both address methodological choices including severity threshold (C70-C72), reaching different conclusions. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting the threshold choice is explained and appropriate. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN as part of broader concerns about not engaging people with CVD in the experimental design, questioning whether the 80% threshold is sufficiently inclusive.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about CVD prevalence, genetic basis, and phenotypes (C1, C10-C21) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/context claims.

OpenEval evaluates literature context claims (C54-C59) as SUPPORTED, noting comparison to Frane's 13.8% finding validates the current study's 12.8% result. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these literature comparison claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological transparency claims (C67-C69, C74-C75) as SUPPORTED, noting clear documentation of temporal scope, bias mitigation strategy, and threshold choices. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methodological documentation claims as a group, though some overlap with R8.
